company_news.headline: Wall Street splits on Big Tech's AI bills
company_news.summary: STORY: :: Central California / July 30, 2026:: AI is costing billions and Wall Street expects returns:: Stephen Nellis, Technology Correspondent"The big takeaway from a spate of big tech earnings this week is that AI costs a lot of money to build, but what Wall Street really cares about is whether you have a credible plan in place to make money off of AI once you've built it.""Microsoft and Meta both talked about spending a lot of money to build up data centers to deliver AI, but one stock, Meta, got punished while another stock, Microsoft, got rewarded. I think what you have to understand is that there's a huge difference in how these companies want to go after AI.""Meta is looking at weaving AI into all of its existing products that people know about, like Instagram, etc.""Microsoft has a bit of a different approach where what they're pitching is saying, hey, what we plan to make money on is that part of helping the business figure out how to apply AI to the data inside their business.""Apple is a little bit different case from the rest of its big tech peers, and that's because at this point, its business is still mostly selling things like iPhones because it's been very late to AI.""The company had really good sales of iPhones and Macs in the quarter that just ended in late June, but looking ahead to the quarter that we're in currently in the rest of the year, it's actually signaling that this AI data center build out is really gumming up the supply chain in a way that's gonna make it harder for Apple to actually build its consumer devices, even though those devices don't compete directly with these data centers.""And I think you're seeing the market respond to what they think of those different approaches."

That may soon become a reality.Amazon-owned Zoox has won the first U.S. approval for commercial deployment of a robotaxi built without traditional human controls.The approval came from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, or NHTSA...allowing the company to begin charging for rides in Las Vegas once it completes state requirements.Here's NHTSA administrator Jonathan Morrison."Since our standards get into performance requirements for specific aspects such as braking performance, they provided information and we received public comment, and we made that determination that their vehicle as equipped, can meet all of those requirements and in fact, exceed those."The vehicle looks very different from a conventional car.It's an electric, carriage-style robotaxi with two rows of inward-facing seats and a top speed of 75 miles per hour.Federal officials say Zoox can deploy up to 2,500 vehicles in each of the next two years.The move comes as companies including Alphabet's Waymo and Elon Musk's Tesla race to expand driverless ride-hailing services across the U.S.The green light comes with added oversight.U.S. regulators say the firm must report issues including crashes and inappropriate stops.Authorities also retain the power to revoke the exemption if major safety concerns emerge.
